item.title: 🔄 How bystanders learn to sustain a blamer
item.description:
A vampire checks the mirror after a feeding. The glass stays empty. Without a reflection to show the blood or the hunger, the vampire looks around for the source of the mess. The blank surface directs the fault toward the furniture, the lighting, or the people standing nearby.

This blindness functions as a closed circuit. When a person cannot register their own image, they lose the ability to locate fault within themselves. They search for a problem and find only a void where accountability should live. This void pushes blame outward. Every mistake becomes a problem caused by the environment or the people in it. Everyone nearby becomes a target.

item.title: 🪞 Reflected motives: The structure of a critique
item.description: A person who fears being seen as controlling may fixate on a colleague who starts sentences with “we should” and who ends meetings one beat early. The colleague may only be organized. To the person watching, every polish lands as overreach. They rehash the same vignette for days, escalate small disagreements, and leave the conversation sure they have drawn a clean moral line. Someone who struggles with dishonesty can spiral the same way: a single missing detail becomes a hunt for proof that others lie. The reaction can feel like moral clarity.
